title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives, find the maximum sum of a contiguous non-empty subarray where you are allowed to delete at most one element from it. Solve it with a two-state Kadane-style dynamic programming pass and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Maximum Subarray Sum with One Deletion

s1_definition.profdef: This problem extends the maximum subarray sum by allowing the removal of at most one element from the chosen contiguous subarray. It is solved in linear time with a two-state dynamic programming pass: at each position we track the best subarray sum ending there with no deletion used and the best subarray sum ending there with exactly one deletion used, updating both from their predecessors, and we take the global maximum across both states.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a trading desk's daily profit and loss and wants the most profitable continuous run, but this time he is allowed to strike out one single terrible day as if it never happened. As he walks day by day he keeps two tallies: the best run ending today if he has not yet used his one strike-out, and the best run ending today if he has already spent his strike-out, always remembering the best of either.
s1_definition.oneliner: Carry two running sums, one with no deletion and one with a deletion already used, and update each from the other.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem extends the maximum subarray sum by allowing the removal of at most one element from the chosen contiguous subarray. It is solved in linear time with a two-state dynamic programming pass: at each position we track the best subarray sum ending there with no deletion used and the best subarray sum ending there with exactly one deletion used, updating both from their predecessors, and we take the global maximum across both states.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a trading desk's daily profit and loss and wants the most profitable continuous run, but this time he is allowed to strike out one single terrible day as if it never happened. As he walks day by day he keeps two tallies: the best run ending today if he has not yet used his one strike-out, and the best run ending today if he has already spent his strike-out, always remembering the best of either.

**One line to remember:** Carry two running sums, one with no deletion and one with a deletion already used, and update each from the other.

sections.s2_technical:
The allowance to delete one element adds a second dimension to the Kadane state. For each index we maintain two quantities. The first, call it `noDel`, is the maximum sum of a subarray ending at this index that uses no deletion. The second, call it `oneDel`, is the maximum sum of a subarray ending at this index that uses exactly one deletion somewhere within it.

The transition for the no-deletion state is ordinary Kadane: `noDel = Math.max(nums[i], noDel + nums[i])`, meaning either start fresh at this element or extend the previous no-deletion run. The one-deletion state has two ways to arrive. Either we extend a run that already used its deletion by adding the current element, which is `oneDel + nums[i]`, or we delete the current element from the best no-deletion run ending at the previous index, which is simply the previous `noDel` value because removing the current element leaves exactly that run. So `oneDel = Math.max(oneDel + nums[i], prevNoDel)`, where `prevNoDel` is the no-deletion value before we overwrote it this iteration.

The ordering matters: we must compute the new `oneDel` using the previous `noDel`, so we snapshot the previous `noDel` before updating it, or compute `oneDel` first. The senior-level nuance is understanding that deleting the current element from a run ending at the previous index is captured precisely by carrying forward the previous no-deletion sum, which is the clever part that keeps the whole thing linear rather than requiring us to try every deletion explicitly.

We track a global maximum across both states at every index, seeding carefully so the subarray remains non-empty, typically `noDel = globalMax = nums[0]` and `oneDel = 0` or negative infinity depending on whether a single-element subarray with a deletion is meaningful; to keep the subarray non-empty we treat the one-deletion state as unavailable until there is at least one element to delete from a longer run. The time complexity is linear, O(n), and the space complexity is O(1). This two-state pass is the standard template for at-most-one-modification subarray problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a trading desk wants a fair view of a strategy's best continuous profit run, but recognizes that a single catastrophic outlier day, perhaps caused by a one-off operational error, can unfairly ruin an otherwise excellent run. Risk management therefore allows the analysis to exclude at most one single day from the chosen run, to see the best run the strategy could have produced without its single worst interruption. This is exactly the maximum subarray sum with one deletion problem.

Problem 2 — Explicitly trying every possible deleted day inside every possible run is cubic or quadratic and does not scale across the desk's histories. The two-state Kadane pass computes the answer in a single linear scan by cleverly encoding the deletion as carrying forward the no-deletion sum, which makes the nightly fair-performance computation feasible.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `ResilientStreakAnalyzer` service with a `bestStreakWithOneExcludedDay` method implementing the two-state pass, and a runnable `MaxSubarrayOneDeletionDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's profit-and-loss sequences, logging the two states at fine level and the best resilient streak at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's profit-and-loss sequence is 1, -2, 0, 3. We seed the no-deletion state at the first element, 1, the one-deletion state as unavailable (treated as negative infinity), and the global maximum at 1.

Step 1 at index 1, value -2: the previous no-deletion was 1. The one-deletion state can arrive by deleting the current element from the previous no-deletion run, giving 1, or by extending an already-deleted run which is still unavailable, so one-deletion becomes 1. The no-deletion state becomes the larger of -2 and 1 plus -2 which is -1, so no-deletion becomes -1. Best here is the larger of -1 and 1, which is 1. Global maximum stays 1.

Step 2 at index 2, value 0: the previous no-deletion was -1. The one-deletion state is the larger of deleting the current element giving -1, or extending the deleted run 1 plus 0 which is 1, so one-deletion becomes 1. The no-deletion state becomes the larger of 0 and -1 plus 0 which is -1, so no-deletion becomes 0. Best here is the larger of 0 and 1, which is 1. Global maximum stays 1.

Step 3 at index 3, value 3: the previous no-deletion was 0. The one-deletion state is the larger of deleting the current element giving 0, or extending the deleted run 1 plus 3 which is 4, so one-deletion becomes 4. The no-deletion state becomes the larger of 3 and 0 plus 3 which is 3, so no-deletion becomes 3. Best here is the larger of 3 and 4, which is 4. Global maximum becomes 4.

The best resilient streak for Rajesh is 4, achieved by taking the run 1, -2, 0, 3 and deleting the single -2, leaving 1, 0, 3 which sums to 4.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem extends the maximum subarray sum by letting me delete at most one element from the chosen contiguous subarray, and I solve it in linear time with a two-state dynamic programming pass. At each position I carry two running values: the best subarray sum ending there with no deletion used, and the best subarray sum ending there with exactly one deletion already used. The answer is the global maximum taken across both states over the whole array.

The no-deletion state follows ordinary Kadane, either starting fresh at the current element or extending the previous no-deletion run. The one-deletion state can be reached in two ways: either I extend a run that already spent its deletion by adding the current element, or I delete the current element from the best no-deletion run ending at the previous index, which is captured exactly by carrying forward the previous no-deletion sum. That second transition is the clever heart of the solution, because it encodes deleting the current element without ever having to try deletions explicitly, which is what keeps the whole pass linear. The one subtlety is ordering: I compute the one-deletion state from the previous no-deletion value, so I snapshot it before overwriting.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on a trading desk. We wanted a fair view of a strategy's best continuous profit run while acknowledging that a single catastrophic outlier day, often a one-off operational error, could unfairly wreck an otherwise strong run, so risk management allowed excluding at most one day from the chosen run. The two-state Kadane pass computed that outlier-tolerant best run in a single linear scan, scaling across the desk's long histories in the nightly report.

The senior-level point I make is that this is Kadane lifted into two states, and the general pattern extends naturally to at-most-k deletions by carrying k plus one states, which shows I see the structure rather than a one-off trick. I also stress the snapshot-ordering detail, because computing the one-deletion state after already overwriting the no-deletion state is the classic bug, and I mention guarding the one-deletion state as unavailable until a real deletion is possible so the subarray stays non-empty. Explaining the generalization and the exact ordering pitfall is what signals genuine command of the technique to an interviewer.
